newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech surgeons remove malignant tumour from Havel.
newsitem.headline: Czech surgeons remove malignant tumour from Havel.

text.p: Czech surgeons removed a small malignant tumour from President Vaclav Havel and took out half of his right lung on Monday, but indicated he might be back at work early in the New Year.
Havel's spokesman Ladislav Spacek said that the operation on Monday morning had gone without complications.
"Doctors believe that the illness has been caught in an early stage," he said in a statement. "The prognosis for the post-operative stage and convalescence is favourable."

Havel, a 60-year-old who has smoked heavily since his youth, was admitted to hospital a week ago after he had failed to throw off a persistent illness. His wife Olga died in January of cancer, aged 62.
Surgeon Pavel Pafko, who led the operating team, said Havel could be back at home soon after the radical surgery which removed half of his right lung.
"If everything goes well...Mr President will remain in hospital for a week to ten days," he told a news conference.

Asked when Havel could resume his duties, he said: "The average time of convalescence with (non-manual) workers after an operation like the one Mr President has undergone is about six weeks. However, it differs a lot from case to case."

The convalescence period for a non-manual worker was about six weeks, he said. Havel had smoked one of his last cigarettes with Health Minister Jan Strasky, another heavy smoker, in hospital at the weekend, he added.
Havel, a small, nervous man, is widely admired at home and internationally for his struggle against communism in which he was jailed many times in the late 1970s and 1980s.

In late 1989 the dissident playwright proclaimed the end of communism to hundreds of thousands of cheering Czechs in Prague as the non-violent "Velvet Revolution" swept him into the presidency of what was Czechoslovakia.
Under his leadership Czechoslovak democracy, twice extinguished this century by Nazi Germany and the Communists, was restored and the country set about rebuilding a market economy.

In late 1992 he resigned rather than preside over the division of the nation into separate Czech and Slovak republics. But early the following year parliament re-elected him to a five-year term as president of the Czech Republic alone.
Unlike Russian President Boris Yeltsin, who underwent heart surgery last month, Havel kept his full presidential responsibilities during the operation.
Under the Czech constitution, most executive power lies with Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus who is attending the European security summit in Lisbon in Havel's place.
Havel's power lies more in his personal authority and reputation for honesty in a Czech political scene increasingly dominated by squabbling and allegations of impropriety.
Opinion polls show his popularity rating at around 80 percent while public disillusionment with politics is widespread.
